name: Future Careers and AI Opportunities
objectives: Given the fields that are growing with AI, identify which growing fields fit your military experience, naming at least two with a reason from your service

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Careers that are growing with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name four kinds of careers growing with AI and say which fit your experience.
This lesson builds toward: Given the fields that are growing with AI, you will identify which growing fields fit your military experience, naming at least two with a reason from your service.
AI is not only creating jobs for programmers. It is changing work in many fields, and it creates demand for people who can run, protect, fix and supervise the systems around it.
Fields where veterans often fit: cybersecurity (protecting networks and data), data and IT support (keeping systems and data running), logistics and supply chain (planning, forecasting, moving goods), skilled maintenance and technician work (equipment, energy, aviation, electronics), and project and operations management (leading people and plans).
Many of these jobs still need hands, judgment and trust. A logistics specialist who can read an AI forecast and then decide what to order is worth more than one who cannot.
Words to know:
- Cybersecurity: protecting computers, networks and data from attacks.
- Supply chain: all the steps that get goods from a maker to the user.
Try it now: Write the five fields from this lesson. Next to each, write one thing you did in service that fits it, or "none yet".
You can now name careers growing with AI and say which fit your military experience.

check.q: Why is AI creating demand for people in some fields?
options: AI runs itself and needs no one
Only robots work in those fields now
Someone has to run, protect, fix and supervise AI systems
AI has replaced all technical jobs
check.why: As AI spreads, people are needed to run, protect, fix and supervise the systems.

check.q: You managed radio and network equipment in service. Which growing field do you write next to it?
options: Cybersecurity or IT support
None, because radio skills do not transfer
Only farming
Only jobs that need no experience
check.why: Network and equipment experience fits growing fields like IT support and cybersecurity.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Matching your MOS, rating or AFSC to civilian jobs
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use official crosswalk tools to list civilian jobs that match your military job.
This lesson builds toward: Given your MOS, rating or AFSC, you will use the O*NET Military Crosswalk and CareerOneStop to list civilian jobs that match your military job, with at least five matching jobs.
Do not start with a guess. Start with the official match. The Department of Labor's O*NET OnLine has a Military Crosswalk Search: choose your branch, type your code or title (for example an Army or Marine MOS, a Navy or Coast Guard rating, an Air Force AFSC or a Space Force SFSC), and see matching civilian occupations.
The Department of Labor's Find a Job page for veterans also links to CareerOneStop's Veterans Job Matcher, which connects military occupations to civilian careers. Use both and keep the jobs that show up more than once.
Then use an AI assistant to understand the list: "Explain these three jobs in plain words, what a normal day looks like, and which of my skills transfer. I was a Navy logistics specialist for 8 years."
Step by step:
- Open the O*NET Military Crosswalk Search.
- Choose your branch and type your code or title.
- Write down the matching civilian jobs.
- Repeat in CareerOneStop's Veterans Job Matcher.
- Ask an AI assistant to explain the jobs that appear on both lists.
Words to know:
- Crosswalk: a tool that matches a military job to civilian jobs.
- Occupation: a type of job, such as logistician or network administrator.
Official sources:
- O*NET OnLine: Military Crosswalk Search
- U.S. Department of Labor VETS: Find a job
Try it now: Look up your military job in the O*NET Military Crosswalk. Pick five matching civilian jobs, then ask an AI assistant to explain each in two plain sentences.
You can now use official crosswalk tools and an AI assistant to list and understand civilian jobs that match your service.

check.q: What does the O*NET Military Crosswalk give you?
options: Your VA disability rating
Civilian jobs that match your military job code or title
A list of open job ads near you
Your GI Bill balance
check.why: The crosswalk matches military job codes and titles to civilian occupations.

check.q: You found five matching jobs but some names are unclear. What do you do?
options: Drop every job with an unclear name
Pick the one with the longest name
Guess what each job is
Ask an AI assistant to explain each one in two plain sentences
check.why: AI is good at explaining a job in plain words once official tools gave you the list.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Exploring a career with an AI assistant
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to describe a career's daily work, skills and entry path, and mark what needs checking.
This lesson builds toward: Given one career from your list, you will use an AI assistant to describe the career's daily work, skills and entry path, and mark every fact that needs checking, marking every number, certification and requirement.
An AI assistant is a good research partner for the first look. Ask it to describe a day in the job, the top skills, the usual tools, common entry-level titles, and the questions you should ask someone who does the job.
Use a clear prompt. Example: "I am an Air Force veteran with 6 years in aircraft maintenance. Explain the job of wind turbine technician: a typical day, top 5 skills, which of my skills transfer, and the usual entry path. Use short bullets."
Mark every fact that can change, such as pay, certification names and requirements, with a question mark. You will check those in the next chapter.
Step by step:
- Pick one job from your list.
- Ask for a typical day, top skills, transferable skills and entry path.
- Ask: "What questions should I ask someone who does this job?"
- Put a question mark next to pay, certifications and requirements.
Words to know:
- Entry path: the usual way people get into a job: training, certification, apprenticeship or degree.
- Transferable skill: a skill from one job that is useful in another.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to describe one career from your list using the example prompt. Put a question mark next to every number, certification or requirement in the answer.
You can now use an AI assistant to explore a career and mark which facts you must check.

options: The usual way people get into a job
The front door of a company
The pay for a first-year worker
The last step before retiring
check.why: An entry path is the usual route into a job, such as training, a certification or an apprenticeship.

check.q: The AI says a career "requires a Security+ certification". What do you do?
options: Sign up for the test right away
Ignore the whole answer
Put a question mark next to it and check it with an official source
Copy it into your plan as fact
check.why: Certifications and requirements are facts to check, not to trust from the AI.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Choosing and planning your path

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Comparing careers with official data
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare three careers' pay, outlook and entry education using the Occupational Outlook Handbook.
This lesson builds toward: Given three careers, you will compare their median pay, job outlook and entry education using the Occupational Outlook Handbook, with every number taken from bls.gov/ooh, not from the AI.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics Occupational Outlook Handbook (bls.gov/ooh) is free and official. For each occupation it gives median pay, the education usually needed to enter, the on-the-job training, and the job outlook: how fast the number of jobs is expected to grow or shrink.
Make a simple table with your three careers in rows and these columns: median pay, entry education, training, job outlook, and your skill gap. An AI assistant can build the empty table for you; you fill in the numbers from the Handbook.
Median pay is the middle point: half of workers earn more, half earn less. Pay also changes by location, so use it to compare careers, not as a promise.
Step by step:
- Go to bls.gov/ooh and search each career.
- Write down median pay, entry education, training and job outlook.
- Write your skill gap: what you still need.
- Put it all in one table.
Words to know:
- Median pay: the middle pay: half of workers earn more and half earn less.
- Job outlook: how much the number of jobs is expected to grow or shrink.
- Skill gap: the skills or credentials you still need for a job.
Official sources:
- Bureau of Labor Statistics: Occupational Outlook Handbook
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for an empty comparison table with your three careers and the columns from this lesson. Fill in the numbers yourself from bls.gov/ooh.
You can now compare careers using official pay, education and outlook data.

check.q: Where do the numbers in your comparison table come from?
options: The AI assistant's answer
A friend's guess
A job ad from one company
The Occupational Outlook Handbook at bls.gov/ooh
check.why: The AI can build the empty table, but the pay and outlook numbers come from official data.

check.q: One career pays more but has slow growth; another pays a bit less and is growing fast. What do you do?
options: Always choose the higher pay
Compare pay, outlook and training together with your own fit
Choose the one with the shorter name
Let the AI choose for you
check.why: Comparing several columns together, plus your fit, gives a better choice than one number.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Finding training and benefits that pay for it
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find one training option for your chosen career and one official program that may help pay for it.
This lesson builds toward: For the career you choose, you will find one training option and one official program that may help pay for it, with one eligibility rule copied from the program's official page.
Several official programs can help. The GI Bill can pay for many schools and training programs; the VA's GI Bill Comparison Tool helps you compare them. VET TEC 2.0 pays for certain non-degree high-tech training (programming, data, information science) for eligible veterans and service members, with a limited number of places each year.
Still in uniform? DoD SkillBridge lets service members train with an industry partner during their last 180 days of service, with command approval. Apprenticeships let you earn while you learn. The Department of Labor's American Job Centers (find one on CareerOneStop) give veterans priority of service for job training.
Eligibility rules change. Ask the AI to list options, then confirm every one on va.gov, dol.gov or with a counselor before you count on it. The VA's Personalized Career Planning and Guidance program gives free counseling to eligible veterans.
Step by step:
- Name the training your career needs (certification, course, apprenticeship).
- Check GI Bill options with the GI Bill Comparison Tool.
- If it is a tech career, read the VET TEC 2.0 page.
- Still serving? Ask your transition office about SkillBridge.
- Confirm eligibility on va.gov or with a counselor.
Words to know:
- GI Bill: VA education benefits for veterans and service members.
- SkillBridge: a DoD program to train with an industry partner during your last 180 days of service.
- Apprenticeship: a paid job with structured training, so you earn while you learn.
Official sources:
- VA: About GI Bill benefits
- VA: VET TEC 2.0
- U.S. Department of Labor VETS: Find a job (SkillBridge, American Job Centers)
- VA: Personalized Career Planning and Guidance
Try it now: For your top career, write one training option and one program that may help pay for it. Open that program's official page and write down one eligibility rule.
You can now find training for a career and an official program that may help pay for it, and confirm the rules.

options: A school that only teaches online
A loan you must pay back
A paid job where you train and earn at the same time
A test you take once
check.why: An apprenticeship lets you earn while you learn.

check.q: You found a program that may pay for your training. What do you check before counting on it?
options: One eligibility rule on the program's official page
Whether a friend used it
Whether the AI said you qualify
Nothing; all veterans qualify
check.why: Eligibility rules are on the official page; AI and friends can be wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing your 90-day career plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a 90-day plan with three dated steps toward one chosen career.
This lesson builds toward: Using your comparison and training choice, you will write a 90-day career plan with three dated steps, with every step specific, dated and including one training or benefit option.
You know how to plan a mission backward from the objective. Do the same here. Choose one career from your table, then plan backward: what must be true in 90 days, 60 days and 30 days?
Good steps are specific and dated: "By 15 November: talk to one person who works as a logistician." "By 1 December: apply for the training program." "By 15 January: apply to five jobs." Vague steps like "look into it" do not get done.
An AI assistant can turn your notes into a clean plan and suggest steps you missed. You decide the dates and you own the plan. Share it with a mentor, counselor or a TAP or American Job Center staff member who can hold you to it.
Step by step:
- Choose one career from your comparison table.
- Write what must be true in 90 days.
- Plan backward: 60-day and 30-day steps.
- Make each step specific and dated.
- Ask AI to format it and suggest anything missing.
- Share it with someone who will check on you.
Words to know:
- Backward planning: starting from the goal and working back to today.
- Milestone: a checkpoint that shows you are on track.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page career plan with three careers, their pay and outlook from bls.gov/ooh, your skill gaps, your chosen career, and three dated steps for the next 90 days including one training or benefit option.
You can now turn career research into a dated 90-day plan you can act on.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Matching careers The careers were guessed or came only from an AI answer. Three careers that match the military job, found in the O*NET Military Crosswalk or CareerOneStop. The learner can say which skill from service fits each career. Official data Pay or outlook is missing or was copied from the AI. Each career has median pay and job outlook from bls.gov/ooh. Entry education is also listed, and the learner explains which career wins and why. Skill gaps No skill gap is listed, or it is vague. Each career lists the skill or credential still needed. Each gap is checked against an official or employer source. Training or benefit No training or benefit option, or one taken only from AI. One training option and one program that may help pay, with one eligibility rule from its official page. The learner also names who to ask to confirm eligibility, such as a VA counselor. 90-day plan Steps are vague or have no dates. Three specific, dated steps toward one chosen career. The plan names a mentor or counselor who will check progress. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Doing your steps in random order
Starting from your goal and working back to today
Planning only for the past
Letting someone else set your dates
check.why: Backward planning starts with the goal and works back to the steps you take now.

check.q: Which is the best step for your 90-day plan?
options: "Think about IT someday"
"Look into stuff"
"Get a good job"
"By 15 Jan: finish the free IT support course module 1"
check.why: A good step is specific and has a date you set.
